title: State v. Pagliai
description: Whether parties in a criminal case can, by plea agreement, confer on the district court the authority to assess costs in dismissed cases, where the plaintiff argues they can and the defendant argues the court lacks statutory authority.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that parties can bargain for the assessment of costs in dismissed cases, relying on precedents that allow for the apportionment of costs in multicount trial information with a conviction.
defendant_argument: Pagliai argued that the district court lacked statutory authority to assess costs in dismissed cases, making the dispositional orders invalid.
decision_outcome: The court conditionally vacated the convictions, sentences, and dispositional orders, remanding the case for the State to elect between vacating only the cost assessment orders or vacating the entire plea bargain and convictions.

title: State Public Defender v. Iowa District Court for Scott County
description: Whether a district court has a role in determining if a local public defender is experiencing a temporary overload of cases, which would allow the public defender to return cases to the court.
plaintiff_argument: The State Public Defender argued that the local public defender has sole authority to determine if a temporary overload exists and can return cases to the court, which the court must accept.
defendant_argument: The Iowa District Court for Scott County, through the attorney general, argued that the court has a role in determining if a temporary overload exists and acted within its discretion to deny withdrawal motions, especially when no other attorneys were available.
decision_outcome: The court sustained the State Public Defender's writ of certiorari, vacating the district court's orders that denied the Davenport Public Defender's motions to withdraw from cases due to temporary overload.

title: State v. Hidlebaugh
description: Whether a district court violates a defendant's constitutional rights to equal protection and due process by imposing a prison sentence based on the defendant's financial inability to meet a plea agreement's condition of purchasing a home, despite good faith efforts.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the district court should adhere to the plea agreement, which stipulated a prison sentence if Hidlebaugh failed to purchase a house by the sentencing date.
defendant_argument: Hidlebaugh argued that his imprisonment resulted from his financial inability to buy a house despite good faith efforts, making his sentence unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment and Iowa Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' decision, vacated Hidlebaugh's sentence, and remanded the case for resentencing, ruling that the sentence violated equal protection and due process principles.

title: State v. Woods
description: Whether there is a federal or state constitutional right to carry a firearm while simultaneously in the illegal possession of a controlled substance or while committing an indictable offense.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Iowa argued that there is no federal or state constitutional right to carry a firearm while committing a crime, specifically while illegally possessing a controlled substance or committing an indictable offense.
defendant_argument: Kevin Dwayne Woods, Jr. argued that his conviction for carrying a dangerous weapon while illegally possessing a controlled substance violates his federal and state constitutional right to keep and bear arms.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Kevin Woods's conviction for violating Iowa Code section 724.8B, ruling that there is no constitutional right to carry a firearm while committing a crime.

title: State v. Scullark
description: Whether a search of a defendant's fanny pack, which was passed to another person before the defendant was handcuffed, violates the United States or Iowa Constitutions' protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the search of Scullark's fanny pack was a valid search incident to a lawful arrest because it was associated with his person at the time of arrest, regardless of his ability to access it later.
defendant_argument: Scullark argued that the search of his fanny pack was unconstitutional because he could not access it when it was searched, and the search-incident-to-arrest exception should not apply under these circumstances.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals decision and affirmed the district court's order denying Scullark's motion to suppress, thereby upholding the legality of the search.

title: State v. Cole
description: Whether Jordan Kevin Cole's convictions for possessing firearms while under a domestic violence protective order violate his Second Amendment and Iowa Constitution Article I, Section 1A rights, or if he waived these rights by consenting to the order.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Cole waived his constitutional rights to possess firearms by voluntarily consenting to the protective order, which explicitly prohibited him from possessing firearms.
defendant_argument: Cole argued that the firearm prohibition was unconstitutional and that he did not waive his Second Amendment and Iowa Constitution Article I, Section 1A rights, especially since the consent order lacked an express judicial finding of dangerousness.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Cole's convictions for possessing firearms while under a domestic violence protective order but remanded the case for entry of a corrected sentencing order.

title: Sikora v. Iowa
description: Whether sovereign immunity bars a former prisoner's state-law tort claims for money damages arising from wrongful imprisonment by state officials.
plaintiff_argument: Eugene Sikora claims he was wrongfully imprisoned for nearly five months due to a miscalculation of his release date and seeks money damages, arguing that sovereign immunity should not bar his constitutional tort claims or common law claims against individual state employees.
defendant_argument: The State of Iowa and its Department of Corrections director argue that sovereign immunity generally precludes state-law tort claims for money damages arising from wrongful imprisonment, and no exception applies, especially after the Burnett decision overruled Godfrey.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Eugene Sikora's tort damages suit for wrongful imprisonment, ruling that sovereign immunity bars such claims against the state and its employees.

title: State v. Amble
description: Whether Iowa Code section 808.16, which declares curbside garbage as abandoned property, is constitutional and allows for warrantless searches, with the State arguing it is constitutional and defendants arguing it is unconstitutional as a violation of privacy rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Iowa Code section 808.16 is constitutional, making curbside garbage abandoned property and thus not protected by Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, allowing warrantless searches.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Iowa Code section 808.16 is facially unconstitutional, violates the separation of powers, and that warrantless trash searches violate a citizen's reasonable expectation of privacy under Article I, Section 8.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's ruling, holding that Iowa Code section 808.16(3) is constitutional and that curbside garbage is abandoned property, allowing warrantless searches.

title: Rivas v. Brownell
description: Whether the supreme court possessed emergency powers to toll the statute of limitations during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the plaintiff arguing it did and the defendants arguing it did not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the supreme court's supervisory order tolling the statute of limitations was constitutional and valid, and therefore her lawsuit was timely filed.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the supreme court lacked the power to toll the statute of limitations, asserting that the tolling provision violated the separation of powers and their due process rights, making the plaintiff's lawsuit time-barred.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's order of dismissal and remanded the case, ruling that the plaintiff's lawsuit was timely filed due to the valid tolling provision.

title: League of United Latin American Citizens of Iowa v. Pate
description: Whether LULAC has standing to challenge a thirteen-year-old permanent injunction and seek an interpretation of the Iowa English Language Reaffirmation Act regarding the dissemination of non-English voting materials.
plaintiff_argument: LULAC argued it had standing to dissolve the King injunction and sought a declaration that the Act, correctly interpreted, allowed non-English voting materials under the rights exception, claiming the injunction impaired its voter mobilization efforts and diverted resources.
defendant_argument: The Secretary of State argued LULAC lacked standing because it did not suffer a legally cognizable injury, its claims were procedurally improper, and the Act required all official voting materials to be in English without applicable exceptions.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court reversed the district court's decision, ruling that LULAC lacked standing to bring the suit and remanded the case for dismissal.

title: State v. Mumford
description: Whether a drug detection dog's momentary intrusion into a vehicle's open window during a lawful traffic stop constitutes an unconstitutional search under the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, and whether there was sufficient evidence to support a conviction for possession of marijuana.
plaintiff_argument: Mumford argued that the traffic stop and the drug dog's sniff, particularly its brief intrusion into the vehicle's cabin, violated her constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures, and that there was insufficient evidence to prove the substance was marijuana.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the traffic stop was lawful, the drug dog's sniff (even with a de minimis intrusion) did not violate constitutional rights, and there was sufficient circumstantial evidence to support the conviction for possession of marijuana.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Iowa affirmed Mumford's convictions, upholding the denial of her motion to suppress evidence and finding sufficient evidence for possession of marijuana.

title: In re N.S.
description: Whether Iowa Code section 724.31, which outlines the procedure for restoring firearm rights after an involuntary mental health commitment, survives strict scrutiny under Amendment 1A of the Iowa Constitution, and specifically whether Amendment 1A shifts the burden of proof from the petitioner to the State.
plaintiff_argument: N.S. argued that Amendment 1A, which makes the right to bear arms a fundamental right subject to strict scrutiny, requires the burden of proof to be shifted to the State to demonstrate that he is currently dangerous, and that section 724.31 is unconstitutionally overbroad as applied to deny his restoration petition without evidence showing he is currently dangerous. He also argued he met the statutory criteria for restoration.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Amendment 1A does not apply retroactively to N.S.'s 2006 commitment, and section 724.31 survives strict scrutiny because the State has a compelling interest in preventing gun violence and suicide, and the statute is narrowly tailored by prohibiting gun ownership by a narrow class of dangerous individuals while providing a restoration process where the petitioner bears the burden of proving they are no longer a threat.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court affirmed the district court's denial of N.S.'s petition for restoration of his firearm rights, holding that Iowa Code section 724.31 survives strict scrutiny under Amendment 1A and that Amendment 1A does not shift the burden of proof to the State.

title: State v. Miller
description: Whether the sentencing of a juvenile offender to a minimum term of incarceration before parole eligibility violates the Iowa Constitution, and whether expert testimony is constitutionally required for such a sentence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that minimum terms for juvenile offenders are constitutional, expert testimony is not required for sentencing, and the district court properly exercised its sentencing discretion.
defendant_argument: Miller argued that minimum terms for juvenile offenders are unconstitutional, or if allowed, require expert testimony from the State, and that the district court abused its discretion by presuming a minimum term and misapplying factors.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court affirmed the district court's sentence of life imprisonment with the possibility of parole after serving thirty-five years, rejecting Miller's constitutional and abuse of discretion claims.

title: State v. Bauler
description: Whether the United States or the Iowa Constitution was violated when a K-9 handler and his trained canine momentarily made contact with the exterior of a vehicle while performing an open-air dog sniff.
plaintiff_argument: The open-air dog sniff, involving physical contact by the dog and handler with her vehicle without a warrant, constituted an unconstitutional search under both the Fourth Amendment and the Iowa Constitution.
defendant_argument: The dog sniff was lawful because dog sniffs are "sui generis" and only reveal contraband, and momentary contact with the vehicle's exterior does not constitute an unconstitutional search or trespass.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of Bauler's motion to suppress, upholding her convictions and sentence.

title: State v. White
description: Whether the use of a one-way closed-circuit television system for child witness testimony, where the defendant could see the witnesses but the witnesses could not see the defendant, violated the defendant's right to face-to-face confrontation under the Iowa Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the one-way video testimony procedure for child witnesses was permissible under Iowa Code and did not violate the defendant's constitutional confrontation rights, citing necessity to protect minors and existing precedent.
defendant_argument: White argued that the Iowa Constitution's confrontation clause requires face-to-face testimony with two-way visibility, and the one-way video system violated this right.
decision_outcome: The court reversed White's convictions and remanded for a new trial, holding that the one-way video testimony violated his confrontation rights under the Iowa Constitution.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc, et al. v. Kim Reynolds, et al.
description: Whether a law prohibiting abortion after a fetal heartbeat is detected is constitutional under the Iowa Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional and the defendant arguing it is constitutional under rational basis review.
plaintiff_argument: The fetal heartbeat statute violates the due process clause, inalienable rights clause, and equal protection clause of the Iowa Constitution, and a temporary injunction should block its enforcement.
defendant_argument: The district court applied the wrong constitutional test; abortion is not a fundamental right under the Iowa Constitution, so the statute should be reviewed under the rational basis test and is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's order granting a temporary injunction, allowing the fetal heartbeat statute to take effect, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Smith v. Iowa District Court for Polk County
description: Whether the Iowa Constitution supports a legislative privilege that protects legislators from compelled document production related to legislation, and if so, whether that privilege is absolute or qualified and applies to communications with third parties.
plaintiff_argument: The nonparty legislators argued that the Iowa Constitution provides an absolute legislative privilege protecting them from compelled document production, even for communications with third parties, and that their intent is irrelevant to LULAC's claims.
defendant_argument: LULAC argued that if a legislative privilege exists under Iowa law, it is qualified and should be abrogated in this case due to compelling constitutional rights at stake, and that discovery into individual legislators' intent is highly relevant to their First Amendment claim.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's judgment granting LULAC's motion to compel and remanded with instructions to quash the subpoenas, thereby ruling in favor of the nonparty legislators.

title: Iowa Individual Health Benefit Reinsurance Association v. State University of Iowa
description: Whether state universities are required members of the Iowa Individual Health Benefit Reinsurance Association (IIHBRA) and subject to its assessments, whether the statutory assessment scheme violates Article VII, Section 1 of the Iowa Constitution, and whether IIHBRA is entitled to late payment fees and attorney fees.
plaintiff_argument: IIHBRA argued that the universities are statutorily required members, the assessment scheme is constitutional, and it is authorized to impose late payment fees and recover attorney fees.
defendant_argument: The universities argued they are not IIHBRA members, the statutory scheme violates the Iowa Constitution by making the state a surety, and IIHBRA lacks authority to assess late payment fees or attorney fees.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that the universities are IIHBRA members and the statutory scheme is constitutional, reversed the denial of late payment fees, and affirmed the denial of attorney fees, remanding for judgment including late payment fees.

title: Livingood v. City of Des Moines
description: Whether the City of Des Moines' use of the state's income offset program to collect automated traffic citation penalties not reduced to a judgment is lawful, with plaintiffs arguing it is unlawful and unconstitutional, and the city arguing it is authorized by statute.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contended the city's use of the income offset program was an unlawful property tax, violated the statute of limitations, amounted to an unconstitutional taking, was preempted by state law, violated their state constitutional right to due process of law, and constituted unjust enrichment.
defendant_argument: The city contended its use of the income offset program to collect ATE penalties was an alternative means of involuntary enforcement explicitly authorized by statute, and that the penalties fell within the meaning of "any liability" or "other qualifying debt" and its conduct was entirely lawful.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, dismissing plaintiffs' claims regarding statute of limitations, unconstitutional taking, and procedural due process, but reversing the dismissal of Livingood's preemption claim for declaratory and injunctive relief and reversing the summary judgment for the city regarding Maury and Robbins' unjust enrichment claim, remanding for further proceedings.

title: Valdez v. West Des Moines Community Schools
description: Whether the district court erred in overruling the plaintiff's Batson challenge to a peremptory juror strike and in granting a directed verdict for the defendant on individual liability for discrimination and wrongful discharge.
plaintiff_argument: Valdez argued the district court erred by overruling her Batson challenge to the peremptory strike of the only Black potential juror and by granting a directed verdict for Johnson, asserting Johnson should be individually liable for constructive discharge under the Iowa Civil Rights Act and common law.
defendant_argument: Defendants contended their peremptory strike of Juror 13 was race-neutral and that Johnson was not individually liable as she lacked supervisory authority to effectuate adverse employment actions or correct a hostile work environment.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the district court, upholding its rulings on the Batson challenge, individual liability, and evidentiary matters.

title: Planned Parenthood of Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds
description: Whether the permanent injunction against the enforcement of Iowa Code chapter 146C's "fetal heartbeat" provision should be dissolved and the statute judicially revived.
plaintiff_argument: The fetal heartbeat bill is unconstitutional under the undue burden standard, which remains the governing law, and an unconstitutional law ceases to exist and must be reenacted by the legislature. Therefore, the injunction should not be dissolved.
defendant_argument: There has been a substantial change in law, particularly after Dobbs, which means rational basis review should apply to abortion laws, making the fetal heartbeat bill constitutional. Therefore, the injunction should be dissolved.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court was evenly divided, resulting in the district court's ruling (denying the State's motion to dissolve the permanent injunction) being affirmed by operation of law. The fetal heartbeat bill remains enjoined.

title: State ex rel. Attorney General of Iowa v. Autor
description: Whether the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act's requirement that civil enforcement actions "shall be by equitable proceedings" violates the constitutional right to a jury trial, with the plaintiff arguing it does not and the defendants arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that civil actions under the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act (CFA) are equitable proceedings, and therefore, defendants are not entitled to a jury trial, even when monetary remedies are sought.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the CFA's requirement for equitable proceedings is unenforceable because it violates the constitutional right to a jury trial, especially since the Attorney General was seeking substantial monetary remedies.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision to strike the defendants' jury demand, ruling that CFA civil actions are equitable in nature and do not inherently require a jury trial.

title: Burnett v. Smith
description: Whether the Iowa Supreme Court should continue to recognize a standalone cause of action for money damages under the Iowa Constitution for alleged constitutional violations, specifically whether the precedent set in Godfrey v. State should be overruled, with the plaintiff arguing for the continued recognition of such claims and the defendant arguing for their abolishment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Cory Burnett, argued that his passive noncooperation during a vehicle inspection did not provide probable cause for his arrest for interference with official acts, and that his constitutional tort claim for damages under Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution should be endorsed, consistent with the precedent of Godfrey v. State.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Phillip Smith and the State of Iowa, argued that Godfrey v. State was wrongly decided and should be overruled, contending that the district court's grant of summary judgment in their favor was correct because there is no direct constitutional tort claim for damages without legislative authorization.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, overruling Godfrey v. State and concluding that a standalone cause of action for money damages under the Iowa Constitution is no longer recognized unless authorized by common law, an Iowa statute, or the express terms of a constitutional provision.

title: State v. Abu Youm
description: Whether the warrantless entry into Abu Youm's apartment was justified under the emergency aid doctrine, or if it violated his Fourth Amendment and state constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures.
plaintiff_argument: The warrantless entry into his apartment was unlawful under the Fourth Amendment and article I, section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, and all evidence obtained should be suppressed as fruit of the poisonous tree.
defendant_argument: The warrantless entry was lawful under the emergency aid doctrine, which is a branch of the community caretaking exception to the warrant requirement.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the court of appeals and the district court judgment, upholding Abu Youm's convictions.

title: LS Power Midcontinent, LLC v. State
description: Whether qualified would-be competitors in the electric transmission market lacked standing to challenge new legislation that blocks them from bidding against existing Iowa operators on future projects.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued they had standing to challenge the constitutionality of anticompetitive legislation (ROFR) because future projects were imminent and they were qualified bidders, and that the ROFR violated the single-subject, title, and equal protection provisions of the Iowa Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing because there were no approved projects to upgrade Iowa's electric grid when the suit was filed, and that the ROFR legislation was constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals decision, reversed the district court's judgment, and remanded the case for the district court to decide the constitutional claims on the merits, granting a temporary injunction to stay enforcement of the challenged legislation.

title: State v. Sallis
description: Whether an officer's recollection of a motorist's barred driving status from several months prior constitutes reasonable suspicion for a traffic stop, and whether a trial court can regulate limited appearances of retained counsel in cases with appointed counsel.
plaintiff_argument: Sallis argued that the officer's information about his barred license was 'stale' and insufficient for a traffic stop, and that the denial of his retained attorney's limited appearance violated his constitutional right to counsel.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the officer had reasonable suspicion for the stop based on prior knowledge of Sallis's barred license, and that the trial court has discretion to regulate limited appearances, especially with appointed counsel, to maintain an orderly process.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Sallis's conviction and sentence, ruling that the traffic stop was justified by reasonable suspicion and the denial of limited appearances was within the trial court's discretion.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds ex rel. State
description: Whether a 24-hour waiting period for abortion violates the Iowa Constitution's single-subject rule and whether a prior ruling establishing a fundamental right to abortion (PPH II) has issue preclusive effect, preventing the state from re-litigating the constitutionality of abortion waiting periods.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued that the 24-hour waiting period legislation violated the single-subject rule and that the prior PPH II decision, which invalidated a 72-hour waiting period, had issue preclusive effect, barring the State from re-litigating the constitutionality of abortion waiting periods. They also argued that mandatory delay laws do not change people's minds and impose significant burdens.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the 24-hour waiting period legislation did not violate the single-subject rule, as both provisions pertained to 'medical procedures'. They also contended that issue preclusion does not apply because the 24-hour waiting period is not identical to the 72-hour period in PPH II, and a state's highest court is not barred from revisiting broad constitutional questions. The State asked the court to overrule PPH II.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's summary judgment, concluding that the 24-hour waiting period legislation did not violate the single-subject rule and that issue preclusion did not apply. The court overruled PPH II, rejecting the fundamental right to abortion under the Iowa Constitution, and remanded the case for further proceedings to determine the appropriate constitutional standard.

title: Landowners v. South Central Regional Airport Agency
description: Whether the 28E Agreement, which created the South Central Regional Airport Agency (SCRAA), is unconstitutional because it binds future legislative bodies and unlawfully restricts Mahaska County's ability to terminate its delegation of powers.
plaintiff_argument: The Landowners and Mahaska County argued that the 28E Agreement is unconstitutional because it binds future boards of supervisors in their legislative functions and prevents the County from exiting the agreement in the same manner it entered.
defendant_argument: The Cities of Pella and Oskaloosa argued that the 28E Agreement is valid, allows for the delegation of governmental functions, and does not unconstitutionally bind future legislative bodies.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the Cities, declaring Article XI of the 28E Agreement invalid and severing it, thereby allowing Mahaska County to withdraw from the SCRAA.

title: State v. Price-Williams
description: Whether law enforcement had reasonable suspicion to order Price-Williams out of a vehicle and conduct a pat-down, and whether his admission to possessing a firearm should be suppressed due to a lack of Miranda warning, with Price-Williams arguing his rights were violated and the State arguing the officer had reasonable suspicion.
plaintiff_argument: Price-Williams argued that law enforcement lacked reasonable suspicion to order him out of the vehicle and pat him down, violating his Fourth Amendment and Iowa constitutional rights, and that his admission about the firearm was obtained through custodial interrogation without a Miranda warning.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the officer had reasonable suspicion to justify ordering Price-Williams out of the vehicle and conducting a pat-down for weapons, and that the Miranda claim was not separately relied upon.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Iowa affirmed the court of appeals decision and district court judgment, upholding Price-Williams's conviction.

title: State v. Hauge
description: Whether law enforcement acted unreasonably under the Fourth Amendment and Iowa Constitution by ordering a passenger out of a vehicle and conducting a pat-down search, and whether the passenger's consent to the pat-down was voluntary.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the officer's order for Hauge to exit the vehicle was necessary to facilitate a lawful arrest of another passenger, and that Hauge's consent to the pat-down was voluntary without requiring an advisement of the right to refuse.
defendant_argument: Hauge argued that law enforcement lacked justification to order him out of the vehicle and that his consent to the pat-down was not voluntary because he was not informed of his right to decline the search.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, ruling that the officer's order for the passenger to exit the vehicle was necessary for a lawful arrest and that the passenger's consent to the pat-down was voluntary.

title: State v. Basquin
description: Whether the Iowa Supreme Court's COVID-19 supervisory orders, which allowed written felony guilty pleas in lieu of in-person colloquies, violated due process and separation of powers, as argued by the defendant, or if the court had the constitutional and inherent authority to issue such orders without violating these principles, as argued by the State.
plaintiff_argument: Basquin argued that the court's supervisory orders allowing written felony guilty pleas violated rules of criminal procedure, precedent, due process, and separation of powers, requiring an in-person plea colloquy.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the court had constitutional and inherent authority to permit written guilty pleas to felonies during the pandemic, and that its supervisory orders did not violate due process or separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court upheld its supervisory orders as lawful exercises of its constitutional and inherent authority during the pandemic, rejecting Basquin's due process and separation of powers challenges, and affirmed his conviction.

title: State v. Lilly
description: Whether Kenneth Lee Lilly's right to an impartial jury under the United States and Iowa Constitutions was violated due to the systematic exclusion of African-Americans from jury pools.
plaintiff_argument: Lilly argued that his right to an impartial jury was violated because neither his jury nor the jury panel contained any African-Americans, and this underrepresentation was due to systematic exclusion caused by the jury selection process, specifically the source lists used.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Lilly failed to prove that the challenged practice of using voter registration, driver's license, and nonoperator identification lists caused the systematic exclusion, especially as it is a 'run-of-the-mill' practice under the Sixth Amendment, and he lacked evidence for his premises under the Iowa Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's holding that Lilly failed to prove a violation of his right to an impartial jury and affirmed his conviction.

title: State v. Wright
description: Whether a peace officer engaged in general criminal investigation without a warrant can take a citizen's opaque trash bags left outside for collection, open them, and rummage through their contents, with the plaintiff arguing such actions violate constitutional rights and the defendant arguing the trash was abandoned and not protected.
plaintiff_argument: Officer Heinz's warrantless search of his trash bags violated his constitutional rights under both trespass and reasonable expectation of privacy theories, especially given local ordinances restricting who can collect trash.
defendant_argument: Wright abandoned his trash, thus losing any reasonable expectation of privacy or property interest, making the warrantless search lawful and not a trespass or an unreasonable search, as local ordinances were for public health, not privacy.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the warrantless search and seizure of Wright's trash bags violated Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution and remanded the case for a hearing to suppress the evidence obtained from the trash pulls.

title: Godfrey v. State
description: Whether Christopher J. Godfrey, an openly gay appointed state official, was subjected to sexual-orientation discrimination and retaliation under the Iowa Civil Rights Act and had his constitutional due process rights violated by Governor Branstad's actions, including a salary reduction.
plaintiff_argument: Godfrey argued that Governor Branstad's decision to request his resignation and reduce his salary was motivated by his sexual orientation, constituting discrimination and retaliation under the Iowa Civil Rights Act (ICRA). He also claimed a constitutionally protected property interest in his salary, which was violated.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued they were entitled to judgment as a matter of law because the ICRA was inapplicable (Godfrey was an officer, not an employee), there was insufficient evidence that Governor Branstad knew Godfrey was gay, Godfrey did not engage in statutorily protected activity for retaliation, and Godfrey had no constitutionally protected property interest in his salary.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the district court and remanded the matter for the entry of dismissal of the plaintiff's claims, ruling in favor of the defendants on all claims.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds
description: Whether the Iowa General Assembly's law, which prohibits abortion providers from participating in federally funded sex education grant programs, violates constitutional rights such as equal protection, due process, free speech, and free association.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland (PPH) argued that the Act violates its equal protection rights by unconstitutionally distinguishing between abortion providers and non-providers, and that it imposes unconstitutional conditions on the receipt of government funds by forcing PPH to give up its rights to free speech, free association, and a due process right to provide abortions.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the funding conditions are rationally related to its interest in selecting the messenger for its programs, expressing a preference for childbirth over abortion, ensuring its message is not diluted, and avoiding indirect subsidization of abortion providers. The State also contended that an abortion provider lacks a freestanding constitutional right to provide abortions, and the Act does not affect a woman's ability to obtain an abortion.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court reversed the district court's order, upholding the state law that prohibits abortion providers from receiving federal grant funding for sex education programs.

title: Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement v. State
description: Whether the State of Iowa has an affirmative duty under the public trust doctrine to protect navigable waters from agricultural nonpoint source pollution, and whether the plaintiffs have standing to compel the State to enact mandatory pollution controls.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the State of Iowa violated the public trust doctrine by failing to protect the Raccoon River from agricultural pollution, leading to increased water treatment costs and impaired recreational use, and seek a mandatory remedial plan.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the plaintiffs lack standing because their alleged injuries are speculative and not redressable by the court, and the issue is a nonjusticiable political question that should be resolved by the legislative branch.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's order, concluding that the plaintiffs lacked standing and the issue was a nonjusticiable political question, and remanded with instructions to dismiss the petition.

title: State v. Sewell
description: Whether Iowa law or the Iowa Constitution guarantee a suspected drunk driver the right to a private phone consultation with counsel before deciding whether to take a blood alcohol test.
plaintiff_argument: Sewell argues that Iowa law and the Iowa Constitution guarantee a suspected drunk driver the right to a private phone consultation with counsel before deciding on a blood alcohol test.
defendant_argument: The State argues that Iowa law does not provide a right to a private phone consultation, and the Iowa Constitution's right to counsel does not attach at the pre-prosecution chemical testing stage.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Sewell's conviction and sentence, concluding he was not entitled to a private phone consultation with counsel under Iowa law or the Iowa Constitution.

title: State v. Treptow
description: Whether Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7, which restrict direct appeals for guilty pleas and mandate postconviction relief for ineffective assistance of counsel claims, are constitutional and whether David Treptow has established "good cause" for a direct appeal.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7 are constitutional, do not violate separation of powers, equal protection, or due process, and that Treptow has not established "good cause" to pursue a direct appeal.
defendant_argument: David Treptow argues that Iowa Code sections 814.6(1)(a)(3) and 814.7 violate the separation-of-powers doctrine, his constitutional right to equal protection, and his right to due process, and that he has "good cause" to appeal due to a lack of factual basis for a conviction.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed David Treptow's appeal, concluding he failed to establish good cause for a direct appeal and that the court lacked jurisdiction, thereby upholding the constitutionality of Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7.

title: Hrbek v. State
description: Whether Iowa Code section 822.3A, which prohibits represented postconviction-relief applicants from filing pro se supplemental documents, is applicable retrospectively and constitutional, or if it violates the separation of powers doctrine and an applicant's right to file such documents.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, John Hrbek, argued that the new law should not be applied retrospectively to his pending case and that it is unconstitutional, violating the separation of powers doctrine and his constitutional right to file pro se supplemental documents.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Iowa, argued that the new law applies prospectively to all filings after its effective date, is constitutional, and does not violate the separation of powers or any constitutional right to hybrid representation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's order, ruling that Iowa Code section 822.3A applies to Hrbek's case and is constitutional, rejecting his claims that it violates the separation of powers or any constitutional right to file pro se supplemental documents.

title: State ex rel. Dickey v. Besler
description: Whether a citizen has standing to bring a quo warranto action challenging the timeliness of a judicial appointment when the appointing authorities (Governor and Chief Justice) have both accepted the appointment as timely, and whether such a challenge is justiciable.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor failed to make a timely appointment, so Besler unlawfully holds office, and Dickey has standing as a citizen to challenge it, making the issue justiciable.
defendant_argument: Dickey lacks standing, the Governor's appointment was timely, and the court should not intervene due to principles of comity and separation of powers, rendering the issue nonjusticiable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, concluding that the case presents a nonjusticiable controversy because both the Governor and the Chief Justice deferred to and accepted the view that the appointment was timely.

title: State v. Thompson
description: Whether the district court erred in admitting evidence of Thompson's residential address and whether Iowa Code section 814.6A, which prohibits represented defendants from filing pro se documents, violates the separation of powers doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: Thompson argued that the residential address evidence was irrelevant and unfairly prejudicial, and that Iowa Code section 814.6A violates the separation of powers doctrine by impeding the appellate courts' essential functioning and a defendant's right to present legal claims.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the residential address evidence was relevant to prove Thompson's knowledge and intent, and that Iowa Code section 814.6A is a proper exercise of the legislature's constitutional authority to regulate court practice and procedure.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Thompson's convictions for attempting to obtain a prescription drug by deceit and rejected his constitutional challenge to Iowa Code section 814.6A, denying his motion to accept a pro se supplemental brief.
